items.title: Hanshan and Shide
items.summary:
A modern retelling of a classic Zen legend

The post Hanshan and Shide appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.
items.content:
It was during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, they say, so in the West the early 7th century and in Japan about the time what are called era names were about to be made. There was, I’m told, a government official called Lu Qiuyin. Some say, though, there likely was no such person. Why, Lu is said to have become Chief Censor of Taizhou, but his biography doesn’t appear in the Tang Book, new or old. The chief censor is the same as the supreme administrator of zhou (“state”) and the supreme administrator of jun (“county”). The entire land of China was divided into dao (“region”), each dao divided into zhou or jun, and each of these divided into xian (“prefecture”), each xian into xiang (“districts”), and each xiang into li (“villages”). The head of a zhou was called cishi, that of jun, taishou. That in Japan calling what’s smaller than xian (“ken”) jun (“gun”) is improper, Mr. Yoshida Tōgo complains. If Lu was Chief Censor of Taizhou, he was an official comparable to Japan’s prefectural governor and as such must appear in the Tang Dynasty Biographies. But without Lu this story won’t go very far, so we assume that he did exist.

Now, it was the third day after Lu came and took office in Taizhou. In Chang’an he had been covered by the dust of North China while drinking muddy water, but now in Taizhou he trod on the fertile land of Central China and drank clear water, so he was in an excellent mood. In addition, for the last three days a great many lower officials had come for an audience with him. Each reported, as a matter of formality, on the business he was charged with. In the midst of all this bustle, he savored a local administrator’s great power, and he was exhilarated.

On the previous day he had told a subordinate that he would get up early in the morning and depart for the Guoqing Temple in Tiantai Prefecture. While in Chang’an he had decided to do this as soon as he arrived in Taizhou. 

For what business did he want to go to the Guoqing Temple? There was a reason for that. When he was appointed Chief Censor in Chang’an and was about to leave for the assigned place, Lu was unexpectedly stricken with an unbearable headache. It was a simple rheumatic headache, but Lu was a nervous sort under the best of circumstances, so took the medicine prescribed by his usual doctor but he still couldn’t get rid of it. “Well, we might have to postpone the day of our departure,” he wondered to his wife, when a maid came in and said, “Sir, there’s a beggar bonze at the front gate and he says he wants to see the master of this house. What shall I tell him, sir?”

“Hmm, a bonze you say,” Lu replied. He thought awhile. “I don’t know, but I’ll see him. Let him in.” Then he made his wife leave the room.

For the higher civil service examinations Lu had only read the Confucian classics and learned to compose five-character-aline quatrains, but he had never read Buddhist sutras or studied Laozi. Yet, for some reason he had respect for people like Buddhist priests and Daoists. Shall we call it the blind respect for something one doesn’t comprehend? And so he said he’d see the bonze.

The man who soon came in was a tall monk. He wore a dirty, tattered robe, and his hair was long, cut only above his eyes. It appeared he had let his hair go until it grew down over his eyes and annoyed him. He held an iron bowl in his hand.

The monk stood wordless, so Lu asked, “I was told you wanted to see me. What can I do for you?”

The monk said, “I have heard you are going to Taizhou. I also hear you are suffering from a headache. I thought I might cure it for you, so came here.”

“You are quite right. Because of this headache I’m thinking of postponing the day of our departure. But how do you propose to cure it? Do you have some formula for me?”

“No. The diseases that trouble our body of the Four Elements are all illusions. Just this alms bowl of clean water will do. I’ll cure your headache with magic.”

“I see, you do magic,” said Lu, and after giving it a little thought, said, “That shouldn’t be any problem. All right, do some magic on me.” This was because he never gave deep consideration to the Way of Medicine and had no definite views on which treatment to take or which treatment to reject, basing his judgment on his own reasoning on each occasion. Because he was like that, even the doctor he usually called on wasn’t someone he had picked through careful selection. He had not sought out someone who read Basic Questions and Spiritual Axis, but decided on one who lived close by and was convenient to summon, and so he hadn’t expected to get any proper medicine. Now he decided to turn to a beggar bonze because the bonze somehow looked distinguished and his bearing made him trust him; also, he thought that magic with a bowl of water at its worst couldn’t do much harm. It’s just the same as high-ranking government officials in Tokyo relying on Safflower Treatment and the Shout Method.

Lu called a maid and told her to take the bowl and fill it with water fresh from the well. The water came. The monk received it, held it up to his chest, and stared at Lu. It could have been clean water or dirty water, hot water or tea. This time it wasn’t dirty, fortunately for Lu. While the monk stared at him for some time, Lu unconsciously focused on the bowl the monk held.

That moment the monk took a sip from the iron bowl and abruptly sprayed it onto Lu’s head.

Lu was astonished. Cold sweat rose on his back.

“Your headache?” asked the monk.

“Oh? It’s gone!” In fact, till then he’d been so concerned about his headache, the headache, that he couldn’t get rid of it, but now, distracted by the bonze’s water, he just let it slip away.

The monk quietly emptied the remaining water on the floor. No sooner had he said, “Now you will excuse me,” than he turned his back on Lu and started walking toward the door.

“Wait, wait a minute,” Lu called out.

The monk turned. “Something else, sir?”

“I’d like to give you something to express my gratitude.”

“No. I beg alms in order to bring blessings to all living things and to subjugate the arrogant, but I do not accept any fee for treatment.”

“I see. Then I won’t insist. May I ask where you are from?”

“Do you mean where I was last? I was at the Guoqing Temple in Tiantai.”

“I see. You were in Tiantai. What is your name, sir?”

“My name is Fenggan.”

“So you are Fenggan from Guoqing Temple in Tiantai.” As though making an effort to memorize it firmly, Lu knitted his brow. “I am just leaving for Taizhou and I feel very close to you. Let me ask you while we’re at it: Are there any great people in Taizhou I might benefit from meeting?”

“Let me see. Yes, there’s one in the Guoqing Temple whose name is Shide. He in truth is Samantabhadra. Then, to the west of the temple there is a rock cave called Cold Boulder, and in it lives one called Hanshan. He in truth is Manjushri. Now, I must be going.” The monk said this, and left quickly.

Because of these reasons, Lu was leaving for the Guoqing Temple in Tiantai.

On the whole, there are three types of attitude people take toward what’s called the Way or religion. Those absorbed in their professions, spending years and months worried how to get by each day, do not give any thought to the Way. The same is true of readers of books. Of course, if they read books and think deeply, they will not fail to attain the Way. But, even without such thinking, they may fulfill their daily duties. These are utterly indifferent people.

Next, there are people who carefully seek the Way. Some give up all for the Way; some do not neglect any of their daily duties while ceaselessly keeping the Way in mind. Whether they enter Confucianism, Daoism, Buddhism, or Christianity, it’s the same. When these people get involved deeply enough, their daily duties become the Way itself. In short, these are all seekers of the Way.

Midway between these indifferent people and seekers of the Way, there are those who objectively recognize the existence of the Way, who are not quite indifferent to it but not really willing to seek it for themselves, those who think they’re remote from it and have given up on it, but who think there is a separate category of people who are close to it and hold them in respect. Respect exists in any kind of person, but if we are simply to consider those who respect the same object, among the seekers of the Way, those who come behind respect those who are ahead, whereas those who come midway as I’m saying, they respect those whom they do not understand, those they can’t comprehend. There blind respect comes into being. And if your respect is blind, it will be utterly useless even if the object you direct it to happens to be right on target.

Lu changed his robes, got on a litter, and went out of his official residence in Taizhou. He had a retinue of sixty attendants.

It was early winter and there was a little frost. They proceeded north, making a detour along the left bank of the Shifengxi, a tributary of the Jiaojiang. The sky that was cloudy at first cleared at long last, and a pale sun shone on the maples along the bank. Old and young passers-by he came across on the road made way for his litter and knelt down. In the litter Lu was feeling very good. That he, a man in the job of governing local people, was now going to bring formal greetings to men of wisdom, seemed to him like some kind of exploit, and that gave him satisfaction.

It was about sixty li from Taizhou to Tiantaixian. In Japan it would be about six and a half ri. Since Lu had his litter bearers go slowly, it was way past noon when he met the officials from the xian who had come out to welcome him. After resting in the governor’s official residence, he learned over the feast offered that it was another sixty li from there to the Guoqing Temple, the road gradually growing steeper. It would be dark before they reached the place. So Lu decided to stay overnight in the governor’s official residence.

The next morning the governor saw him off. The weather that day was no different from that of the previous day. The proverbial “Tiantai of eighteen thousand zhang” seems a bit too high, no matter who surveyed it or when. Anyway, tigers inhabited the mountain. Unlike the previous day, the progress was slow. They had lunch on the way. It was when the sun was setting in the west that they reached the gate of the Guoqing Temple. It was a temple that Emperor Yang of Sui is said to have built after the death of the Great Teacher Zhiyi.

As the Chief Censor was visiting to pay his respects, the temple wasn’t negligent. A monk called Daoqiao came out to welcome Lu and led him to the guestroom. When the welcoming with tea and cakes was over, Lu asked, “You had a monk called Fenggan in your temple, did you not?”

Daoqiao replied. “You said Fenggan, sir? Yes, he was staying in a monastery behind the main hall until not long ago. But then he went off on pilgrimage and hasn’t returned.”

“What kinds of things did he do while in this temple?”

“Let’s see now. He husked rice for the monks.”

“He did? Wasn’t there something different from the other monks about him?”

“Yes. There certainly was. At first we regarded Fenggan simply as a kindly brother who would avoid no chore, but in time we began to treat him as someone special. But then one day he abruptly left.”

“Tell me what happened.”

“It was an utter mystery, sir. One day he came back from the mountain riding a tiger. And just as he was, he came right into the corridor on the tiger’s back, chanting poems while riding the tiger back and forth. He liked to chant poems very much, and at night he used to chant poems in the monastery in the back.”

“I see. He must be a living arhat. What’s happened to the monastery now?”

“It’s still empty, sir. Occasionally during the night a tiger comes there and roars.”

“I don’t want to trouble you, but would you please take me there?” Lu said, standing up.

Brushing aside the cobwebs with his hands, Daoqiao led the way and took Lu to the empty house Fenggan used. The sun had almost set. They looked around in the house. In the light that was faint, it was vacant, with nothing in it. Daoqiao stooped and pointed at the footprints of a tiger on the stone floor. At that moment a mountain wind happened to blow past outside the window, whirling up the fallen leaves piled up high in the garden. That sound broke the bleak silence noisily. Feeling as though the roots of his hair were suddenly tightened, Lu had goose flesh all over his body.

Lu hastened out of the empty house. And he said to Daoqiao who followed, “Is there a monk called Shide still in your temple?”

Daoqiao had a puzzled expression as he looked at Lu’s face.

“You know so much about us, sir. Only a little while ago, he was warming himself by the fire in the kitchen with a man called Hanshan. If you have something for him to do, shall I summon him, sir?”

“I see. So Hanshan, too, is here, in the kitchen. That is more than I had expected. While I’m troubling you like this, would you take me to the kitchen?”

“Yes, sir,” Daoqiao said, and walked west along the main hall.

Lu, following him, asked, “When did Mr. Shide come to live in this temple?”

“A long time ago I should think, sir. He’s a foundling Mr. Fenggan brought back from the pine woods.”

“I see. And what does he do in the temple?”

“I hear that in the three years since Fenggan brought him from the pine forest, they taught him to burn incense, light candles, offer food, and do other things for the statue in the main altar in the kitchen, so I’m told. But then I heard that one day he was found eating face to face with the statue after putting offerings on the altar. It appears that he did it because he didn’t know how much respect he should pay to Pindola Bharadvaja. Now we make him do the monks’ dishes in the kitchen.”

“You do,” Lu said and walked a few steps before he asked, “You also mentioned Hanshan. What kind of person is he?”

“Hanshan, you say. He lives west of this temple, in a stone cave we call Cold Rock. When Shide does the dishes he collects the remaining bits of rice and vegetables and stores them in a bamboo tube, which Hanshan comes to collect.”

“I see,” Lu said as he followed Daoqiao. If Hanshan and Shide who do such things were Manjushri and Samantabhadra, who could Fenggan riding a tiger be? he wondered, like a rustic fellow at a theater confused as to which actor is playing which role.

“I’m terribly sorry this is really a messy place, sir,” said Daoqiao as he led Lu into the kitchen.

The kitchen was filled with steam, so for Lu who had just stepped in it was almost impossible to see things clearly. In that grayness he saw three large ovens in all with wood still burning red. As he stood there awhile watching, he began to see a host of monks moving rice, vegetables, and soup from pots and kettles to the table built into the rock walls.

Daoqiao looked far into the room and called out, “Hey, Shide!”

As Lu followed his eyes, he saw before the farthest oven from the entrance two monks squatting, warming themselves.

One of them was bare-headed with his hair a few inches long, his feet in straw sandals. The other wore a hat of bark, his feet in wooden clogs. Both were skinny, shabby, small men, unlike Fenggan, who was quite big.

When Daoqiao called out, the bare-headed one turned his head and grinned, but did not reply. That appeared to be Shide. The one with a hat on didn’t even budge. That must be Hanshan.

Or so Lu guessed as he walked up to them. He formally held his sleeves inward, reverentially bowed, and introduced himself, “I am Lord Steward of the Imperial Council, Provincial Commander-in-Chief, Chief Censor of Taizhou, Army Chief of Staff, with Emperor-bestowed Scarlet Robe and Fish Tally, and I humbly call myself Lu Qiuyin.”

Shide and Hanshan simultaneously glanced at Lu. Then the two looked at each other, uttered laughter that could only have welled up from the pit of their stomachs, rose to their feet, and ran out of the kitchen. As they ran, Lu heard Hanshan say, “Fenggan prattled!”

The monks gathered around Lu, who was startled as he stared in the direction they had disappeared, to distribute rice, vegetables, and soup. Daoqiao stood where he was, deathly pale.

♦

“Hanshan and Shide: A Story by Mori Ōgai,” translated by Hiroaki Sato from Cold Mountain Zen, copyright © 2026 by Hiroaki Sato. Reprinted by permission of New Directions Publishing Corp.

items.title: India’s cockroach movement brought down a minister. Bringing real reform will be much harder
items.summary: The structural issues fuelling anger and frustration among young people have existed for decades. Here’s where the government needs to start.
items.content:
Over the past few weeks, young people have mobilised to protest India’s broken education system, against the background of a shortage of job opportunities.

The protests were initially sparked by the cancellation of a medical school entrance exam after questions were leaked, leading some despondent young people to take their own lives. The movement repurposed the image of a cockroach as their symbol – inspired by a comment by India’s chief justice, allegedly comparing jobless young people to “cockroaches”. Humour and satire were integral to the recent unrest.

On Saturday, the cockroach movement claimed its biggest victory since the protests began with the resignation of India’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

But this move will only do so much. These issues did not appear overnight, nor can they be easily fixed.

Read more: The youth jobs crisis fuelling India’s Cockroach Janta Party protests

Decades of frustration

Irregularities and shortcomings in education, as well as rampant unemployment, have been major issues in northern India since at least the early 1970s. One of the main reasons for this is the economic growth that occurred in the late 20th century was not accompanied by broad-based investment in education. It also failed to create jobs in the private sector, leaving many young people dependent on government jobs.

As I wrote in my book Timepass: Youth, Class and the Politics of Waiting in India, for example, by the late 1990s, thousands of graduates were chasing a single government job in the northern city of Meerut.

In response, many young people engaged in what they called “timepass” – spending time hanging out at street corners while continuing to study for degrees. One set of students started a club called “Generation Nowhere”.

Many of the young people I interviewed were bitter about their predicament. Many could not afford the best schools. The education system was also rife with problems, from the frequent leaks of exam papers to teacher shortages.

When I was doing fieldwork relating to young people and social change in the state of Uttar Pradesh in 2004, I met students satirically campaigning for their “democratic right to cheat” in examinations. Like the young people at the heart of the cockroach movement, these students, too, complained of questions being leaked in advance of exams and the cheating inherent in the educational system.

They also believed talented students were cheated out of a job after graduating because of the scale of unemployment in India. “Why shouldn’t we cheat, when the system is cheating us?”, one student quipped.

Students also said the system of applying for government jobs was unfair. One told me: “Everywhere, you need source [social connections] and force [money power]”.

Today’s distinctive challenges

Young people today have similar feelings of anger and being stuck in limbo. But their daily realities have changed.

As Avishek Jha and Nilanjana Sen, two researchers at the University of Melbourne, recently argued, Indian youth are often channelling considerable effort into preparing for government exams, rather than engaging in “timepass”. This reflects a growing awareness of the real threat of youth unemployment in India and a determination to find ways to maximise their chances.

An enormous number of “tuition centres” or cram schools, coaching centres, and study spaces have emerged to cater to this more driven generation, but the odds stacked against young people in competition for scant government jobs remain the same. Cockroach protesters are frustrated by all the effort and resources they are forced to expend to prepare for exams that don’t ultimately lead to better lives.

This points to the deeper, systemic problems at the heart of India’s massive youth unemployment problem.

Four main issues to address

With their main demands now met by the government, those in the cockroach movement will likely shift their focus to these broader questions of fairness in education and employment.

First, tackling structural educational problems is an obvious priority. This may require decentralising the management of examinations. But as Professor Manisha Priyam pointed out in research in Bihar, the problem is wider than the leaking of examination papers. The government must also better regulate tuition and coaching centres to ensure their marketing and activities are transparent and above board.

Second, many Indian commentators are again emphasising the issue of job creation. The government should also look at ways to improve work-integrated learning to give students better training in key fields.

Another priority is reforming school and university courses so young people can obtain the skills necessary to compete for private and public jobs, while also creating opportunities for themselves through start-ups.

This is linked to a third issue – greater investment in schooling and higher education. Sixty years ago, a commission set up by the government to examine the state of education in India recommended the government increase spending to 6% of gross domestic product (GDP). This hasn’t happened: spending is currently just 4.1%.

Several experts have pointed out that education investment also needs to be smart. It should be targeted at curriculum review, improving the performances of institutions and staff, and speeding up the technological and infrastructural transformation in education.

A final theme emerging from the cockroach movement is the need for Indian authorities across the board to respect and value young people. This starts with a better understanding of the capabilities, talents and skills of those in gen Z.

Where to look for inspiration

Crucially, the cockroach movement is focusing attention on the realities of mainstream, public education – starting in primary schools – rather than simply what is happening in elite institutions.

There are some important initiatives underway that build on India’s National Education Policy. But to take a holistic approach to education reform and job creation, Indian policymakers should also look at developments in other large, developing countries, such as Brazil.

Policymakers must also look at India’s own history of successful community-government partnerships.

Above all, reforms that involve young people should now be the priority. Those in the cockroach movement have demonstrated their desire to become genuine collaborators in education reform. They deserve a seat at the table.

items.title: Julius Caesar by Nick Makoha
items.summary:
I believe that James McAvoy is a type of Caesar. But he never stays

in character long enough to make it hold. Now when pirates had

Caesar caught in a trap off the coast of Rhodes, he demanded that

they ask for more than double the ransom
items.content:
I believe that James McAvoy is a type of Caesar. But he never stays
in character long enough to make it hold. Now when pirates had
Caesar caught in a trap off the coast of Rhodes, he demanded that
they ask for more than double the ransom. When Caesar says,
do this, it is performed. These fishermen, his kidnappers (is “kidnapped”
too strong?), accepted his request as he recited poetry to them on a throne
of flour. Two months after paying the ransom, with the aid of a private

army, he squeezed the yolk out of these men. We’re doomed. I know
we can’t all be Moses but have you noticed that superstars always want to
play our parts. There’s this dialogue where Nicholas Garrigan, played
by McAvoy, is rebuked by Idi Amin—You promised to me you would help me
build a new Uganda. McAvoy doesn’t answer. Don’t you know that that’s
how they take us? It is Bura’s Desperado Sacrifice. Forcing the Black king
to h8 doesn’t seem to accomplish much, but it makes all of the difference

in just two moves. (1. Qxh8 2. Xxa1 Qd4). Crossing a runway is not
like crossing the street, especially when your Black king is a counterfeit
played by Forest Whitaker and his lazy eye. Planes have been hiding in
the air. This duty-free gin is a useless placebo. But rumour has it Miss
America Tawny Godin from Yonkers has a smile you want all to yourself.
The thing about my country is that there is always somebody ready to say
—You’re mine. Maybe I should have led with that. Anyway, it’s your move.

Editor's Note

Listen to Nick Makoha talk about how he burned his suit in order to become a poet in this episode of Wake, Butterfly.

items.title: The Crossing
items.summary: Our first landlady picked up cigarette butts thrown by the next-door neighbors onto the sidewalk, and tossed themback on their deck. We knew it was timeto move when the man who boughther building put up eviction warningnotices on the doors
items.content:
Our first landlady picked up cigarette 
butts thrown by the next-door neighbors 

onto the sidewalk, and tossed them
back on their deck. We knew it was time

to move when the man who bought
her building put up eviction warning

notices on the doors without asking
if the rent checks might have been

misdelivered. Another place we occupied
had no insulation. Winter was a revelation

of plastic sheets ballooning over windows.
Roof rats, water in the basement, faulty

radiators. Once, we thought the crossing
we made would be temporary. We didn't 

imagine we'd dwell in it, longer than any of
the apartments we rented in succession. 

I know I can't ask the future to declare 
itself. I boil water on the stove for tea 

and consider unwritten pages, the shape 
that remaining has pressed into the furniture. 

Not every hour is seeded with difficulty,  but 
the gods continue to collect transit tickets.

items.title: A Monastery Grows in North Bend
items.summary:
Spiritual hunger, interfaith coalitions, and the "New Gandhara” of the West Coast

The post A Monastery Grows in North Bend appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.
items.content:
On a typical weekday morning, two saffron-robed monks walk silently into Pike Place Market, alms bowls in hand to accept gifts of food for their one meal of the day. They touch no money. They have no idea what, if anything, they’ll be offered. And yet in five years of doing this they have not gone hungry a single day.

This is Ajahn Kovilo and Ajahn Nisabho, cofounders of Clear Mountain Monastery, a new Theravada Buddhist forest monastery taking shape on ninety acres of forested land in North Bend, Washington, about forty minutes outside Seattle. Their path to this moment runs through Thailand, India, Myanmar, Goenka meditation halls, and a warm, ongoing partnership with Saint Mark’s Episcopal Cathedral in downtown Seattle. 

“The first day we went downtown, seven people offered food in thirty minutes,” Ajahn Nisabho says. There have been surprising moments too: On one occasion, just when it looked as if they would be fasting for the day: “A homeless guy came out of an alleyway with a box of protein bars and just said, ‘Here.’ ” 

Ajahn Kovilo recalls a Thai monk friend, Ajahn Gai, gently teasing him when Ajahn Nisabho started going daily to the Market. “He said, ‘I am worried about Ajahn Nisabho going for alms at Pike Place Market.’ I said, ‘Why? There are generous people in America too.’ ‘Because they sell fish,’ ” he deadpanned (cue rim shot).

The skepticism, it turned out, was unfounded. Seattle “is the most secular city in the US,” Ajahn Nisabho says, “and we didn’t know how this monastic venture would play out there.” But far from finding indifference, they found hunger—among the young in particular, which runs against the usual pattern found in most convert Buddhist sanghas, which tend to be filled with baby boomers. Their Saturday gatherings, held at Saint Mark’s Cathedral, now draw around 120 people in person, with roughly 100 more joining online, alongside two or three daily Zoom meditation sittings. “The Buddha taught in the vernacular, and the vernacular of this age is social media,” Ajahn Nisabho says. “We’ve found a way of rippling the teachings out through YouTube and other things, and people are so hungry for community.”

That hunger for community is a gap they’re trying to fill in people’s dharma lives, what Ajahn Nisabho calls “the siloed existence that is the endemic problem of convert Buddhism in the US.” Clear Mountain, in their telling, isn’t only a meditation hall; it’s an attempt to build the social architecture of practice, central to which is social potlucks and interfaith connections. “These last five years have been building up that architecture of faith,” he says. “Everything’s offered freely, and support has really come from inspiration.”

The two monks aren’t alone in this. Ajahn Kovilo mentions a constellation of newer Theravada monastic communities that have sprung up and down the West Coast in recent years—a partial list would include Pacific Hermitage in White Salmon; Passaddhi Vihara in Olympia; Parayana in Port Townsend; Dhammadharini in Penngrove, California; and Karuna Vihara in Santa Cruz; these newer monastic communities adding to the old guard, which includes Sitavana in B.C., Abhayagiri in Ukiah, and Metta Forest Monastery near San Diego. 

“The Buddha taught in the vernacular, and the vernacular of this age is social media,” Ajahn Nisabho says. “We’ve found a way of rippling the teachings out through YouTube and other things, and people are so hungry for community.”

Ajahn Kovilo notes how, during a talk at one of their gatherings, the visiting teacher Ajahn Sona, the abbot of Sitavana Monastery in British Columbia, dubbed the whole region the “New Gandhara” —a nod to the ancient cultural crossroads where Buddhism once flourished— “given all the different Theravada monasteries for bhikkhus and bhikkhunis” now established there. The Buddha said that his sasana was not complete unless the “fourfold assembly” of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen was established. By the monks’ count, only two places in the world currently host this kind of full convergence of Theravadin monks and nuns in close proximity: Western Australia, and now, the Pacific Northwest.

After three years of searching, the community found its land six months ago: ninety forested acres in North Bend, within an elk migration corridor and close enough proximity to the city—about forty minutes—to sustain the daily alms practice that defines their way of life. “In Asia, the model depends on being close enough to the city for alms round,” Ajahn Nisabho explains, “so it’s not novel—but it is quite novel for forest monasteries in North America,” most of which sit two or more hours outside any city. The community raised $5 million to purchase the property. The long-term vision, he says, includes housing for up to twenty monastics, a dedicated quarter for visiting bhikkhunis, a lay sala for daily chanting and meditation, a beautiful temple open to day visitors, and a forested portion of the land set aside for monks pursuing deeper solitary practice. “We don’t want to lose that side of things,” he adds.

Ajahn Nisabho’s path to monasticism began close to home. He grew up in Spokane, Washington, the son of Buddhist parents who had studied with the likes of Jack Kornfield. At 15, he read Hermann Hesse’s Siddhartha—”not actually a terribly Buddhist book in its plot arc,” he says, “but it’s archetypal and delicious”—and found something in it that took root. “The vision of the Buddha just shone gold in my heart,” he recalls. “There are a few moments in your life where you step into a footprint that feels like it was made for you—and that was one of them.”

He kept meditating through college and spent time oriented toward social work—including a gap year in Calcutta alongside a doctor working in the slums—before deciding the deeper container of monastic life was what he needed after a visit to Abhayagiri Monastery in California. “I stepped into the silence,” he says, “and realized I really needed that container to face my suffering.” He went on to Thailand, found a teacher in Ajahn Anan at Wat Maphrao, and ordained there.

Ajahn Kovilo came to Buddhism through ten-day Goenka Vipassana retreats—and the realization, as he puts it, “that my life needed more than just a ten-day retreat twice a year.” Digging deeper, he discovered the rich world of teachings in the Pali canon, and, in 2003, began devouring everything he could find on the early online source Access to Insight, much of it the work of the American-born Thai forest monk Thānissaro Bhikkhu (Ajaan Geoff). When he realized Ajaan Geoff was the abbot of an actual monastery in southern California, he gave away his possessions and hitchhiked north with a tent and a rucksack, planning to stay ten days. He stayed a year and a half. (“My last driver for that hitchhike was named Jesus,” he notes, “which seemed auspicious.”)

He was ordained at Abhayagiri in 2010 by Ajahn Pasanno and Ajahn Amaro, then spent six years moving between Thailand and the US—training at a Pa Auk monastery, learning Thai and some Pali, and later spending four years at the Dharma Realm Buddhist University studying Mahayana traditions. Today, both monks describe themselves as part of a wider network of teachers and elders in the Ajahn Chah lineage; Ajahn Nisabho is at work on a biography of Luang Por Pasanno, and Ajahn Kovilo edited Stillness Flowing, the biography of Ajahn Chah by Ajahn Jayasaro.

Around six years ago, after studying with Ajahn Jayasaro and time spent between Wat Maphrao and Abhayagiri, Ajahn Nisabho felt pulled back to the Northwest. “Seattle seemed like it had rich dharma ground,” he says, “and—strangely—no forest monastery. That struck me as the great missing puzzle piece in people’s dharmic lives.” He and Ajahn Kovilo landed in the city—Nisabho first, then Kovilo part-time and eventually full-time—”and just went on faith.”

None of this would have been possible without Saint Mark’s Episcopal Cathedral, which has hosted Clear Mountain’s community gatherings for five years. When Ajahn Kovilo and Ajahn Nisabho first approached the cathedral’s leadership, “we laid out our situation without asking for anything, just saying we wanted to exist in a space of giving if we could.” The response was immediate: A granola bar was offered on the spot, and the simple words, “Yeah, just meet here.” Ajahn Kovilo adds a detail he clearly finds moving: The cathedral is the very place where Luang Por Sumedho, the elder living monastic disciple of Ajahn Chah and early progenitor of the Thai forest tradition in the West, had once served there as an altar boy at age 11—a small thread tying the two traditions together even before the monastery existed.

The relationship has only deepened since. The two communities now hold an annual January lunch, in which Clear Mountain’s community brings a meal to the cathedral staff as a thank-you. And out of ongoing conversation between the two traditions came something more—an interfaith worship service whose name takes inspiration from Thich Nhat Hanh, called “Living Buddha, Living Christ, Living Spirit.”

The Reverend Canon Emily Griffin, who has served as canon vicar of Saint Mark’s since October 2024, traces the service’s origin to a conversation around mid-2023, when Ajahn Nisabho expressed interest in deepening the relationship through shared prayer or worship. A cathedral staff member and a key lay volunteer sat down with the monks to explore what that might look like—and found, perhaps unsurprisingly to anyone familiar with the long history of contemplative exchange between the two traditions, real common ground. “What they discovered,” Griffin says, “was that there were resonances between the perfections of character related to enlightenment in Buddhism and what are called the Fruits of the Spirit in the New Testament.” Around the same time, the cathedral had begun hosting Taizé services—a chant-based, ecumenical style of worship that originated in France—and it became the natural form for the new collaboration to take.

The first service was held in the summer of 2024; the third took place just last week, drawing about 150 people. “What’s beautiful about it is that folks from both traditions walk away feeling their own faith enriched,” Griffin says. “Not only are you appreciating a tradition that’s not your own and valuing the other but you’re seeing your own tradition in greater depth, which is just a gift.”

The exchange runs in both directions. Beyond the Saturday gatherings, Ajahn Nisabho and members of the Clear Mountain community occasionally join Sunday worship at Saint Mark’s, and cathedral members have, in turn, been invited to sit with the monks during meditation. “There’s a wonderful spirit of openness, curiosity, and respect,” Griffin says. “Our relationship has been life-giving and enriching.”

Asked what she felt the monks had brought to her own congregation, Griffin pointed not to doctrine but to a quality of attention. “I think one of the real gifts they bring is the reminder that being fully present is a gift,” she says. “As Episcopalians, we can be a little task-oriented. . . . The emphasis on quality of time and relationship-building has been a real gift to us, and has helped us lean into that—because it’s part of our tradition, too, but in the rush to get things done, we sometimes lose it. The way they embody presence inspires us to do the same.”

Reflecting on my conversation with the ajahns, I was struck by the theme of skillful relationship and community-building that surfaced again and again. “Beautiful friendship is half of the holy life,” Ananda once famously remarked to the Buddha.

“Oh no,” the Buddha replied, “beautiful friendship is the whole of the holy life.”

The post A Monastery Grows in North Bend appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.

items.content:
—the lock cut in two. Now I have to walk
to Our Lady and St. Joseph, through
the sparse needlework of deciduous
branches. It turns out we still need
each other—stranger, maybe
you saw the black and orange chassis
and thought speed, something sleek
to meet the headwinds; maybe warm
meals for the week or a present for someone
you hurt and love; or maybe you’d make
of its handlebars and spokes better use
than I could, as forest floor mycelia
spin carbon, nitrogen from muck—

I was so angry with you. The date I’d planned
for Saturday fell through, a friend
vanished from my life last week.
The fossil news from Baku, bleak, and suffering
in Lebanon, Sudan, Syria, Palestine.
All things that can be taken, what you thought
was yours, that everything changes hands, and I—

I was late. The mass was almost over,
the voices nearly finished with their singing.
Bread, water, some kind of stolen grace
flashed past me on two wheels in the wind.
December was late. Outside the ash
was watching itself end
and time ride with the thief.

items.title: Etude
items.summary: "To be scattered—desire luminousand in tatters—" ~ Robin Coste LewisThis same desire growsstronger each year insteadof finally being sated—the conditionof those like us who tooka chance and stepped acrossa threshold, before understandinghow
items.content:
"To be scattered—
desire luminous
and in tatters—"
                  ~ Robin Coste Lewis


This same desire grows
stronger each year instead
of finally being sated—
the condition

of those like us who took
a chance and stepped across
a threshold, before understanding
how thresholds multiply, ache

following ache. The port recedes, 
and the end of the runway recedes
but the bright edge of cities
cannot eclipse the darkness.

Those who have never had
to leave think of longing 
as a bright, sure progression
toward fullness.

Those who have never been
left behind don't bend
instinctively toward
a secret wound.

A voice; the scent
of roasted corn or the oil
of oranges. Something
accordions into mirage.

I can arrange this kingdom
so it fits entirely on a teaspoon,  
float it like a petal on bath water.
At the end of the winding

mountain road, the houses
huddled together come
into view. Have I lived
everything that is 

supposed to be my life?
I am told I need to be
patient, but when was I
not patient? Rain

has trained me
to be quiet, to undertand
how even a stone can 
wear away with time. 

Still, I turn my face 
toward sunlight, toward 
what gleams with no bitterness, 
without indifference.

items.title: Practice Like the Four Elements
items.summary:
A venerated teacher from the Thai forest tradition on using the elements to train our minds away from its habitual responses.

The post Practice Like the Four Elements appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.
items.content:
A city person may like to eat mushrooms. He asks, ‘‘Where do the mushrooms come from?’’ and someone tells him, ‘‘They grow in the earth.’’ So he picks up a basket and goes walking out into the countryside, expecting the mushrooms will be lined up along the side of the road for him to pick. But he walks and walks, climbing hills and trekking through fields, without seeing any mushrooms. A villager has gone picking mushrooms before, and she knows where to look for them; she knows which part of which forest to go to. But the city person only has the experience of seeing mushrooms on his plate. He heard they grow in the earth and got the idea that they would be easy to find, but it didn’t work out that way.

Training the mind in samadhi, meditative stability, is similar. We get the idea it will be easy. But when we sit, our legs hurt, our back hurts, we feel tired, we get hot and itchy. Then we start to feel discouraged, thinking that samadhi is as far away from us as the sky from the earth. We don’t know what to do and become overwhelmed by the difficulties. But if we can receive some training, it will get easier little by little.

When we are new to it, training in samadhi is difficult. Anything is difficult when we don’t know how to do it. But training at it, this can change. That which is useful can eventually overcome

and surpass that which is not. We tend to become fainthearted as we struggle—this is a normal reaction, and we all go through it. So it’s important to train for some time. It’s like making a path through the forest. At first it’s rough going, with a lot of obstructions, but returning to it again and again, we clear the way. After a while, we have removed the branches and stumps, and the ground becomes firm and smooth from being walked on repeatedly. Then we have a good path for walking through the forest. This is what it’s like when we train the mind. Keeping at it, the mind becomes illumined. The Buddha and his disciples were once ordinary beings, but they developed themselves to progress through the stages of enlightenment. They did this through training.

It’s important to train for some time. It’s like making a path through the forest. At first it’s rough going, with a lot of obstructions, but returning to it again and again, we clear the way.

What was the Buddha’s advice on how to practice meditation? He taught to practice like the earth, to practice like water, to practice like fire, to practice like wind. Practice like the ‘‘old things,’’ the things we are already made of: the solid element of earth, the liquid element of water, the warming element of fire, the moving element of wind.

If someone digs the earth, the earth is not bothered. It can be shoveled, tilled, or watered. Rotten things can be buried in it. But the earth will remain indifferent. Water can be boiled or frozen or used to wash something dirty; it is not affected. Fire can burn beautiful and fragrant things or ugly and foul things—it doesn’t matter to the fire. When wind blows, it blows on all sorts of things, fresh and rotten, without concern.

The Buddha used this analogy. The aggregation that is us is merely a coming together of the elements of earth, water, fire, and air. If you try to find an actual person there, you can’t. There are only these collections of elements. But for all our lives, we never thought to separate them like this to see what’s really there; we have only thought, ‘‘This is me. This is mine.’’ We’ve always seen everything in terms of a self, never seeing that there are merely earth, water, fire, and air. But the Buddha teaches in this way. He talks about the four elements and urges us to see that this is what we are. There are earth, water, fire, and air; there is no person here. Contemplate these elements to see that there is no being or individual, but only earth, water, fire, and air.

It’s deep, isn’t it? It’s hidden deep—people will look but they can’t see it. We’re used to thinking in terms of self and other all the time. So our meditation is still not very deep. It doesn’t reach the truth, and we don’t get beyond the way things appear to be. We remain stuck in the conventions of the world, and being stuck in the world means remaining in the cycle of transformation: getting things and losing them, dying and being born, being born and dying, suffering in the realm of confusion. Whatever we wish for and aspire to doesn’t really work out the way we want, because we are seeing things wrongly. With this kind of grasping attachment, we are still very far indeed from the real path of dharma.

Let’s get to work right now. Our practice of dharma should be getting us beyond suffering. If we can’t fully transcend suffering, then we should at least be able to transcend it a little, now, in the present. For example, when someone speaks harshly to us, if we don’t get angry, we have transcended suffering. If we get angry, we haven’t transcended dukkha.

When someone speaks harshly to us, if we don’t get angry, we have transcended suffering. If we get angry, we haven’t transcended dukkha.

When someone speaks harshly to us, if we reflect on dharma, we will see it is just heaps of earth involved. OK, he is criticizing me—he’s just criticizing a heap of earth. One heap of earth is criticizing another heap of earth. Water is criticizing water. Air is criticizing air. Fire is criticizing fire.

But if we really see things in this way, then others will probably call us mad. ‘‘He doesn’t care about anything. He has no feelings!’’ When someone dies we won’t get upset and cry, and they will call us crazy.

It really comes down to practicing and realizing for ourselves. Getting beyond suffering doesn’t depend on others’ opinions of us, but on our own individual state of mind. Never mind what they will say—if we experience the truth for ourselves, then we can dwell at ease.

When difficulties occur, recollect dharma. Think of what your spiritual guides have taught you. They teach you to let go, to have restraint and self-control, to put things down; they teach you to

strive in this way to solve your problems. The dharma that you study is just for solving your problems.

What kind of problems are we talking about? How about your families? Do you have any problems there? Any problems with your children, your spouses, your friends, or your work? All these things give you headaches sometimes, don’t they? These are the problems we are talking about; the teachings are telling you that you can resolve the problems of daily life with dharma.

We have been born as human beings. It should be possible to live with happy minds. We do our work according to our responsibilities. If things get difficult, we practice endurance. Earning a livelihood in the right way is one sort of dharma practice, the practice of ethical living. Living happily and harmoniously like this is already pretty good.

We are usually taking a loss, however. Don’t take a loss! If you go to a center or a monastery to meditate and then go home and fight, that’s a loss. Do you hear what I’m saying? It’s just a loss to do this. It means you don’t see the dharma even a tiny little bit—there’s no profit at all.

♦

From Everything Arises, Everything Falls Away © 2005 by Ajahn Chah, translated by Paul Breiter. Reprinted in arrangement with Shambhala Publications, Inc. Boulder, CO. www.shambhala.com

items.content:
1

My soul radially whorls out to the edges of my body, according to the same laws
by which stars shine, communicating with my body by emanation.

When you see her, you feel the impact of what visual can mean.

Invisibility comes through of deep pink or a color I see clairvoyantly.

This felt sense at seeing the rose extends, because light in the DNA of my cells
receives light frequencies of the flower as a hologram.

The entire rose, petals in moving air, emotion of perfume records as a sphere, so
when I recall the emotion, I touch dimensionality.

From a small bud emerges a tight wound bundle of babyskin coral petals, held in
a half globe, as if by cupped hands.

Then petals are innumerable, loose, double, sumptuous, unified.

I look through parted fingers to soften my gaze, so slow light shining off the
object is filtered; then with feeling I look at swift color there.

It's swiftness that seems still as noon light, because my seeing travels at the same
speed.

I make a reciprocal balance between light falling on the back of my eye to optic
nerve to pineal gland, radiance stepping down to matter, and my future self
opening out from this sight.

A moment extends to time passing as sense impression of a rose, including new
joys where imagined roses, roses I haven't yet seen or seen in books record as my
experience.

Then experience is revelation, because plants and people have in their cells
particles of light that can become coherent, that radiate out physically and also
with the creativity of metaphor, as in a beam of light holographically, i.e., by
intuition, in which I inhale the perfume of the Bourbon rose, then try to separate
what is scent, sense, and what you call memory, what is emotion, where in a
dialogue like touching is it so vibratory and so absorbent of my attention and
longing, with impressions like fingerprints all over.

I'm saying physical perception is the data of my embodiment, whereas for the
rose, scarlet itself is matter.


2

The rose communicates instantly with the woman by sight, collapsing its
boundaries, and the woman widens her boundaries.

Her "rate of perception" slows down, because of its complexity.

There's a feeling of touching and being touched, the shadings of color she can sense
from touch.

There's an affinity between awareness and blossom.

The rose symbolizes the light of this self-affinity.

I come to visit drooping white cabbage roses at dusk.

That corner of the garden glows with a quality of light I might see when light
shines through mist or in early morning reflects off water.

I stand quietly and allow this quality to permeate air around me.

Here, with a white rose, color is clairsentient, this color in the process of being
expressed, like seeing Venus in the day.

Walking, I move in and out of negative space around which each rose is engaged
and become uncertain of my physical extent as an object.

Look at the energy between people and plants; your heart moves into depth
perception; for depth, read speed of light.

I set my intention through this sense of moving into coherence with the bio-photons
of a plant and generate feeling in response.

A space opens and awareness gathers it in, as at night my dream is colorless and
weaves into the nuance.

I can intentionally engage with the coherence of light beams, instant as though
lightless, or the colored light of a dimension not yet arrived, as our hearts are not
outside affinity with respect to wavelength, shaping meaning, using the capacity
for feeling to sense its potency in a rose and to cultivate inter-being with summer
perfume. 


 

Editor's Note

Listen to Mei-mei Berssenbrugge talk about being a hermit in this episode from the first season of Wake, Butterfly.

items.summary: I wonder what it took to stay the terriblemoment of doubt, and so do the gods’ bidding?Too many instances of sacrifice in mythology,each a dagger entering history in the guise of duty. But surely there was doubt? Some small tremor before th
items.content:
I wonder what it took to stay the terrible
moment of doubt, and so do the gods’ bidding?
Too many instances of sacrifice in mythology,
each a dagger entering history in the guise
of duty. But surely there was doubt? Some
small tremor before the winds of prophecy
named one daughter instead of another,
thrust her neck on a stone altar? Torn
sails mended, boats sailed through pliant
waters as if thresholds were always meant
to be marked with blood. Centuries later,
we are still saying war is the circumstance
that justifies murder. Cities burn, seas turn
their dark into a wine that erases memory.

items.title: Dive bar
items.summary:
beer and cheer and howl
form a neighborhood

the company of others
might be plenty

but many go small
the red of an open mouth

and make a man burst
like a glass full of words
items.content:
Up pretty early (though of late I have been faulty by an hour or two every morning of what I should do) and by water to the Temple, and there took leave of my cozen Roger Pepys, who goes out of town to-day. So to Westminster Hall, and there at Mrs. Michell’s shop sent for beer and sugar and drink, and made great cheer with it among her and Mrs. Howlett, her neighbour, and their daughters, especially Mrs. Howlett’s daughter, Betty, which is a pretty girl, and one I have long called wife, being, I formerly thought, like my own wife. After this good neighbourhood, which I do to give them occasion of speaking well and commending me in some company that now and then I know comes to their shop, I went to the Six clerks’ office, and there had a writ for Tom Trice, and paid 20s. for it to Wilkinson, and so up and down to many places, among others to the viall maker’s, and there saw the head, which now pleases me mightily, and so home, and being sent for presently to Mr. Bland’s, where Mr. Povy and Gauden and I were invited to dinner, which we had very finely and great plenty, but for drink, though many and good, I drank nothing but small beer and water, which I drank so much that I wish it may not do me hurt.
They had a kinswoman, they call daughter, in the house, a short, ugly, red-haired slut, that plays upon the virginalls, and sings, but after such a country manner I was weary of it, but yet could not but commend it. So by and by after dinner comes Monsr. Gotier, who is beginning to teach her, but, Lord! what a droll fellow it is to make her hold open her mouth, and telling this and that so drolly would make a man burst, but himself I perceive sings very well.
Anon we sat down again to a collacon of cheesecakes, tarts, custards, and such like, very handsome, and so up and away home, where I at the office a while, till disturbed by, Mr. Hill, of Cambridge, with whom I walked in the garden a while, and thence home and then in my dining room walked, talking of several matters of state till 11 at night, giving him a glass of wine.
I was not unwilling to hear him talk, though he is full of words, yet a man of large conversation, especially among the Presbyters and Independents; he tells me that certainly, let the Bishops alone, and they will ruin themselves, and he is confident that the King’s declaration about two years since will be the foundation of the settlement of the Church some time or other, for the King will find it hard to banish all those that will appear Nonconformists upon this Act that is coming out against them.
He being gone, I to bed.

beer and cheer and howl
form a neighborhood

the company of others
might be plenty

but many go small
the red of an open mouth

and make a man burst
like a glass full of words


Erasure poem derived from The Diary of Samuel Pepys, Friday 24 July 1663.

items.title: Eaten
items.summary:
the lie eating me
is simple
I believe it in a way

it has the force
of an oven
on soused meat
items.content:
Up and to my office, and thence by information from Mr. Ackworth I went down to Woolwich, and mustered the three East India ships that lie there, believing that there is great-juggling between the Pursers and Clerks of the Cheque in cheating the King of the wages and victuals of men that do not give attendance, and I found very few on board.
So to the yard, and there mustered the yard, and found many faults, and discharged several fellows that were absent from their business.
I staid also at Mr. Ackworth’s desire at dinner with him and his wife, and there was a simple fellow, a gentleman I believe of the Court, their kinsman, that made me I could have little discourse or begin acquaintance with Ackworth’s wife: and so after dinner away, with all haste home, and there found Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten at the office, and by Sir W. Batten’s testimony and Sir G. Carteret’s concurrence was forced to consent to a business of Captain Cocke’s timber, as bad as anything we have lately disputed about, and all through Mr. Coventry’s not being with us.
So up and to supper with Sir W. Batten upon a soused mullett, very good meat, and so home and to bed.

the lie eating me
is simple
I believe it in a way

it has the force
of an oven
on soused meat


Erasure poem derived from The Diary of Samuel Pepys, Thursday 23 July 1663.

items.title: Crafty
items.summary:
who is calling her
but genius
no Christ is ever as light

as a private joy that comes to be
more than pleasure
the country where now is

not staying there
but breaking to put on
other clothes

passing as
a home maker
as her art works
items.content:
Up, and by and by comes my uncle Thomas, to whom I paid 10l. for his last half year’s annuity, and did get his and his son’s hand and seal for the confirming to us Piggott’s mortgage, which was forgot to be expressed in our late agreement with him, though intended, and therefore they might have cavilled at it, if they would.
Thence abroad calling at several places upon some errands, among others to my brother Tom’s barber and had my hair cut, while his boy played on the viallin, a plain boy, but has a very good genius, and understands the book very well, but to see what a shift he made for a string of red silk was very pleasant. Thence to my Lord Crew’s. My Lord not being come home, I met and staid below with Captain Ferrers, who was come to wait upon my Lady Jemimah to St. James’s, she being one of the four ladies that hold up the mantle at the christening this afternoon of the Duke’s child (a boy).
In discourse of the ladies at Court, Captain Ferrers tells me that my Lady Castlemaine is now as great again as ever she was; and that her going away was only a fit of her own upon some slighting words of the King, so that she called for her coach at a quarter of an hour’s warning, and went to Richmond; and the King the next morning, under pretence of going a-hunting, went to see her and make friends, and never was a-hunting at all. After which she came back to Court, and commands the King as much as ever, and hath and doth what she will.
No longer ago than last night, there was a private entertainment made for the King and Queen at the Duke of Buckingham’s, and she was not invited: but being at my Lady Suffolk’s, her aunt’s (where my Lady Jemimah and Lord Sandwich dined) yesterday, she was heard to say, “Well; much good may it do them, and for all that I will be as merry as they:” and so she went home and caused a great supper to be prepared. And after the King had been with the Queen at Wallingford House, he came to my Lady Castlemaine’s, and was there all night, and my Lord Sandwich with him, which was the reason my Lord lay in town all night, which he has not done a great while before.
He tells me he believes that, as soon as the King can get a husband for Mrs. Stewart however, my Lady Castlemaine’s nose will be out of joynt; for that she comes to be in great esteem, and is more handsome than she.
I found by his words that my Lord Sandwich finds some pleasure in the country where he now is, whether he means one of the daughters of the house or no I know not, but hope the contrary, that he thinks he is very well pleased with staying there, but yet upon breaking up of the Parliament, which the King by a message to-day says shall be on Monday next, he resolves to go.
Ned Pickering, the coxcomb, notwithstanding all his hopes of my Lord’s assistance, wherein I am sorry to hear my Lord has much concerned himself, is defeated of the place he expected under the Queen.
He came hither by and by and brought some jewells for my Lady Jem. to put on, with which and her other clothes she looks passing well.
I staid and dined with my Lord Crew, who whether he was not so well pleased with me as he used to be, or that his head was full of business, as I believe it was, he hardly spoke one word to me all dinner time, we dining alone, only young Jack Crew, Sir Thomas’s son, with us.
After dinner I bade him farewell. Sir Thomas I hear has gone this morning ill to bed, so I had no mind to see him.
Thence homewards, and in the way first called at Wotton’s, the shoemaker’s, who tells me the reason of Harris’s going from Sir Wm. Davenant’s house, that he grew very proud and demanded 20l. for himself extraordinary, more than Betterton or any body else, upon every new play, and 10l. upon every revive; which with other things Sir W. Davenant would not give him, and so he swore he would never act there more, in expectation of being received in the other House; but the King will not suffer it, upon Sir W. Davenant’s desire that he would not, for then he might shut up house, and that is true. He tells me that his going is at present a great loss to the House, and that he fears he hath a stipend from the other House privately.
He tells me that the fellow grew very proud of late, the King and every body else crying him up so high, and that above Betterton, he being a more ayery man, as he is indeed. But yet Betterton, he says, they all say do act: some parts that none but himself can do.
Thence to my bookseller’s, and found my Waggoners done. The very binding cost me 14s., but they are well done, and so with a porter home with them, and so by water to Ratcliffe, and there went to speak with Cumberford the platt-maker, and there saw his manner of working, which is very fine and laborious. So down to Deptford, reading Ben Jonson’s “Devil is an asse,” and so to see Sir W. Pen, who I find walking out of doors a little, but could not stand long; but in doors and I with him, and staid a great while talking, I taking a liberty to tell him my thoughts in things of the office; that when he comes abroad again, he may know what to think of me, and to value me as he ought. Walked home as I used to do, and being weary, and after some discourse with Mr. Barrow, who came to see and take his leave of me, he being to-morrow to set out toward the Isle of Man, I went to bed.
This day I hear that the Moores have made some attaques upon the outworks of Tangier; but my Lord Tiviott; with the loss of about 200 men, did beat them off, and killed many of them.
To-morrow the King and Queen for certain go down to Tunbridge. But the King comes hack again against Monday to raise the Parliament.

who is calling her
but genius
no Christ is ever as light

as a private joy that comes to be
more than pleasure
the country where now is

not staying there
but breaking to put on
other clothes

passing as
a home maker
as her art works


Erasure poem derived from The Diary of Samuel Pepys, Wednesday 22 July 1663.

items.title: A Moving Temple
items.summary:
Buddhists gather across New York City for the Day of Remembering Our Interdependence.

The post A Moving Temple appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.
items.content:
On July 12, about one hundred people walked silently and slowly under the bright sun toward the Metropolitan Detention Center (MDC) in Brooklyn, the third stop of the Day of Remembering Our Interdependence pilgrimage. The event, organized by a collective called Mahasangha NYC, called on people of different Buddhist lineages and other faiths to join a walk across the five boroughs of New York, with stops for ritual, chanting, speeches, and community building. 

The group came to a stop across from the MDC, where past visitors had affixed handmade signs saying “Happy Birthday, Dad” and “We Love You” to a chain-link fence. The MDC, the only federal prison in New York, currently holds about 1,200 people, including infamous cases like the former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro. The New York Times has reported on the center’s “dreadful conditions, near perpetual lockdowns, and grave staffing shortages.” Now, the MDC holds hundreds of people detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) during the raids and immigration sweeps of the last eighteen months. 

As Sister True Vow of Blue Cliff Monastery led the group of pilgrims in a song, people inside the prison began banging on the narrow fogged windows, as if to communicate their presence to those outside. “May all live in peace, be protected and safe,” the group sang. Dharma teacher Kaira Jewel Lingo echoed this wish in her remarks: “Every human being in this building behind us is a human being worthy of our love and respect.” Lingo noted she was about the same age as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the man shot and killed by ICE agents in Houston just days before, though the agents were looking for a different person. 

The banging continued as Father Adam Bucko offered a prayer in the Christian tradition, followed by remarks from Rev. Juan Carlos Ruiz, who leads weekly vigils outside the center and works with some of the detainees. People who have been released told him of the horrific conditions inside, which made the notorious Delaney Hall in Newark look like “child’s play.” 

Meanwhile, a team of medics wearing red crosses circulated through the crowd offering water, sunscreen, snacks, and fans. Pilgrimage co-organizer Mara Phelan, who is a doctor, knew that the day would be hot and sunny, so she asked her medically trained friends to volunteer. It was one of many small acts of care for the group, some of whom had been outside since 8:00 a.m. that morning. 

Artist and author Tenzin Mingyur Paldron then took the microphone and spoke about meeting a Tibetan woman who was imprisoned for twenty-seven years by Chinese authorities. While in prison, the woman learned that the Dalai Lama was still alive and wanted to tell her fellow prisoners to give them hope. But the prisoners were isolated and not allowed to speak, so she sang a well-known song with the line, “After the snowfall comes the warmth of the sun.” The others reflected, understood the meaning, and rejoiced—all to the confusion of their guards. “They were trying to contain life,” said Paldron. “And we are uncontainable.” Paldron ended with a series of full-body prostrations in front of the MDC as the group chanted. 

Co-organizer Dorotea Mendoza said the idea for the day came out of a friends gathering in February. Many of them were troubled by the state of the country yet inspired by the Walk for Peace, in which a monastic group traveled barefoot 2,300 miles from Fort Worth, Texas, to the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., over 110 days. “It’s like call and response,” said Mendoza. “That was their call, what is our response?” 

Over many conversations and iterations, the group of about ten organizers, mostly women of color, came up with the idea of staging a similar walk. Like the Walk for Peace, they wouldn’t put forth a political message but would instead insist on their deepest values. “I wasn’t there trying to fix anything,” Mendoza said of being outside the MDC. “That in itself feels light.”  

Some pilgrimage organizers, like Stephanie Cates, had met through activist spaces around environmental justice and Palestine, but Cates felt it was important to “bring others in as our own, even the people that I might consider my enemy, like an ICE agent.” Milou Haskin, another organizer, said the pilgrimage wasn’t about making demands. “We’re not actually waiting on anyone,” she said. “We want to insist on how much we love each other and [take] care of each other—for this little microcosm to embody all the things we want the world to be.”

The Day of Remembering Our Interdependence inspired similar walks that weekend in Austin, Texas; New Orleans, Louisiana; and Troy, New York. Its emphasis on cross-denominational Buddhism echoes the May We Gather memorials in Los Angeles and Antioch, California, which use ritual to bring attention to historic and current anti-Asian violence. And many participants are connected through other cross-lineage networks like the Buddhist Council of New York and Buddhist Action Coalition. 

For the New York pilgrimage, the day began at two separate points: at the 9/11 Memorial on Staten Island, and at the Banana Kelly Double Dutch sculpture in the Bronx, an iconic artwork from 1982 by John Ahearn and Rigoberto Torres. The two groups, using a mix of walking and public transit, converged later that morning at the African Burial Ground National Monument, where two members of the Ramapo Munsee Lenape Nation, Grandmother Clara Soaring Hawk and Owl Steven Dennison Smith, offered blessings. The group then stopped for lunch in Brooklyn before walking to the MDC. Throughout the day, participants were invited to reflect on two questions: What stories does this place hold that I have not yet learned to hear? What would it mean to meet this place with an open heart rather than certainty? 

The event website described it as a “Buddhist-led interfaith” walk where “all are welcome.” Michael Shen, one of the volunteer medics, doesn’t identify as a practicing Buddhist but said, “It was very nice to walk in silence and meditate on our interconnectedness.” He added that it was “heart-wrenching” to hear the taps on the windows of the MDC, which “solidified the fact that there are humans in there,” and that he’s considering returning for the weekly vigils. 

The day’s last stop was the Socrates Sculpture Park in Queens, where organizers had arrived early to set up chairs and a spread of chips, wraps, and pastries. The walkers gathered under the trees overlooking the East River as the sun sank. There was more singing, and speakers emphasized our interdependence with nature and honoring the Lenape Indigenous to the land. Rev. James A. Lynch of the Buddhist Council of New York offered the merit of the day to “those who feel forgotten, abandoned, unseen, or lonely,” among many others. Rev. Doyeon Park of the Won Buddhist community spoke of using the four great vows, including “Sentient beings are numberless; we vow to save them,” as guides for our action, then chanted them in Korean. 

To conclude the pilgrimage, Mendoza held up a jar containing water from Staten Island and the Bronx, and invited fellow organizer and environmental activist Matthew Menzies to lead a ceremony. Menzies spoke about his own experience being born on the East River and his Indigenous roots as a way of naming the complexities of where we come from. “Your home flows within you,” he said, then poured the jar into the river so waters from the five boroughs could mingle. 

Phelan stood by the river with tears in her eyes as the day concluded. “I’d been in organizing spaces before, and something was always missing, so I came to the conclusion that organizing wasn’t for me,” she said. Phelan added that protests were absolutely needed, but the Day of Remembering Our Interdependence showed her what she’d been missing. “I really needed the faith piece, I really needed the Buddhist spiritual piece, I really needed the love. It feels like coming home to find the space where I belong, and the people that I want to organize with.”

items.content:
William Herschel. Good guy with a telescope, not so much
with the lingo: he called his discovery “Georgium Sidus”
or “Georgian Star” after George III, but the name didn’t stick.
In France, where the name of the British king was to be avoided
at all costs, the planet was known as “Herschel” until the name
“Uranus” was universally adopted. But that’s the way it goes:
the biggest mistake you can make is to play a song for a friend
and expect them to love the lyrics as much as you do. There you are,
blinking back tears, while your friend is hoping that an airplane
hits your house so they don’t have to listen to this lugubrious shit
anymore, though lugubrious is a wonderful word, isn’t it,
because it sounds exactly like someone crying but is also funny,
like Buick or waffle. Notice I’m talking about single words here,
not phrases like “Christian bachelorette party.” Or “oblong
farincaceous compound,” which is what Henry James actually
called his waffle in a memoir. Oh, Henry, why couldn’t you
just say “waffle”? No wonder nobody reads you anymore
except me. Nobody remembers the lyrics to songs, either,
which is why at singalongs people say, “Sweet Caroline,
something always seemed so something!” and “When I find
myself in times of something, Mother Mary comes to me”
as well as “Imagine there’s no something.” You remember
talking with your buddies when you were a teenager, right?
Not the substance of the conversation, though, just the talk.
You were becoming unstuck from your family. You wanted
sex, but you weren’t really sure what it was. The jokes
were pure anarchy, and they took place in a car about
the size of a jail cell and just as far from your parents’ world,
from school. I think language is more than capable
of looking out for itself, don’t you? I mean, when was
the last time you looked at the list of synonyms for
baffled? They’re among the best in the English language:
puzzled, nonplused, discombobulated, flummoxed, stumped,
fogged, bewildered, buffaloed. Maybe we should just
shut up. To ban the spread of Covid, during the pandemic
there were signs on Japanese roller coasters asking riders
to “please scream inside your heart.” Maybe we
shouldn’t try to take out old words and add new ones.
I mean, you’d feel stupid if you were outside with
your friends all sweaty and wrung-out after a hootenanny
and someone pointed up to the sky and said, “Look, Herschel.”
